title: Social teaching close
hook: love of neighbor, built into how we live together

segments.voice: Yesterday, social teaching at home: the big letters weighed in small choices. Your line was conscience at the checkout.

A bridge carries strangers across a river all day long, and hardly anyone crossing it thinks about it. Somebody did, once. Somebody calculated the load, the wind, the winter, so that people they'd never meet could get home safely. That's care that doesn't look like care. It looks like steel and paperwork. This block of the path began with a phrase, love, organized, and it ends today with a picture close to that bridge: love of neighbor, built into the way people live together.
screen: `A BRIDGE FULL OF STRANGERS.` → `CARE THAT LOOKS LIKE STEEL.` → `LOVE, BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old command. Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." One person carrying another's load. Catholic social teaching asks a second question: what if the load could be made lighter for everyone, before anyone has to carry it alone? Then two ways to love. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote of the love of one neighbor, face to face, and also an institutional path of charity, where love works through law, economics and politics for the common good. He called that second path no less a form of love than the first. Pope Francis, for his part, speaks of political love, the love that builds a fairer society for people one will never meet. Then the block, added up. Every life. Everyone takes part. Rights and duties. The poor first. Work has dignity. One family. Our common home. Markets have limits. Nothing and no one thrown away. Each one is love of neighbor, set into something that outlasts a single good deed. Last, what it doesn't replace. Benedict was clear that no structure will ever make person-to-person love unnecessary. There will always be someone lonely, someone grieving, someone who needs a face, not a policy. So the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder, and the bridge. Love made structural isn't love made cold. It's love that keeps working after you've gone home.
screen: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · `FACE TO FACE, AND THROUGH INSTITUTIONS.` · `THE BLOCK'S LINES, ADDED UP.` · `STRUCTURES NEVER REPLACE A FACE.` · then, large: `SO YOU SHALL FULFIL THE LAW OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Let a few of the block's lines pass slowly, the poor first, our common home, everyone takes part, and notice which one stays. Then picture one small act tied to it that could keep going without deciding it fresh each time: a monthly gift, a regular shift, a reminder to write to your representative again. If you pray, offer it to God as a promise.

Social teaching close. The block in one picture: love of neighbor, face to face and built into how people live together. Tomorrow a new block begins, on Mary: her feasts, her titles, and what the Church teaches about her.
Your line: love made structural. A hand on the shoulder, and a bridge. That's the block; see you for Mary tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics live social teaching both in direct works of mercy and in longer commitments: volunteering on a schedule, giving regularly, joining parish justice groups, and taking part in public life with the Church's principles in mind.

fork.setup: your street floods every spring and the same neighbors lose everything. you've helped bail out basements for years. what does love made structural add?
options: keep helping, and push for a drain that stops the flood.
fork.reveal: the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder now, and the structure that lightens the load for everyone.

chat.says: If there are good laws and programs for the poor, do we still need to help people ourselves?
options: Yes; Benedict said no structure ever makes person-to-person love unnecessary. The Church asks for both.
No; once love is built into good laws, the Church says personal charity isn't needed.
Yes, because the Church sees laws and programs as cold, so they don't count as love.
chat.meaning: Benedict called the institutional path of charity no less a form of love, yet said no structure makes personal love unnecessary.

Galatians.meaning: the Christians of Galatia, to whom Paul wrote a letter

common good.meaning: the good of everyone together, not only a few

political love.meaning: Francis's phrase for love that builds a fairer society

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older Catholic English translation of the Bible

sources.quoted: Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.

notes: Caritas in Veritate §7 paraphrased: the 'institutional path' of charity, 'no less excellent and effective' than direct charity. Confirm.
Deus Caritas Est §28b paraphrased: there will always be suffering and loneliness that call for personal love; no just order makes charity superfluous. Confirm.
Fratelli Tutti §§180–182 paraphrased on political love / social love. Confirm section numbers.
